docs.title: nave-xai
docs.text:
NAVE explanations of vision encoders: which concepts an encoder extracts, and where.

nave-xai is the official package of NAVE (Neuro-Activated Vision Explanations), from Multi-depth Concept Extraction for Post-Hoc Vision Encoder Explanation (ECML PKDD 2026) by Ahcène Boubekki, Samuel G. Fadel and Sebastian Mair.

NAVE explains the encoder, not a prediction. It combines a frozen encoder's feature activations at several depths, extracts concepts from them, and returns an explanation map of how the encoder decomposes the image, before any classifier. Post-hoc, unsupervised, for CNNs and ViTs.

Citation

If you use nave-xai, please cite the paper:

               and Manco, Giuseppe and Spiliopoulou, Myra and Masciari, Elio},
  title     = {Multi-depth Concept Extraction for Post-Hoc Vision Encoder Explanation},
  booktitle = {Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases. Research Track},
  publisher = {Springer Nature Switzerland},
  address   = {Cham},
  pages     = {449--467},
  year      = {2026},
  doi       = {10.1007/978-3-032-37664-0_26},
  isbn      = {978-3-032-37664-0}

from nave_xai import NAVEImage
exp = NAVEImage().explain(image)
exp.explanation          # (H, W) the concept of every pixel

docs.text:
Bases: _ConceptsBase

NAVE explainer: concepts from a vision encoder, and explanations of images with them.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default model "vitt16" (ViT-Ti/16, the default), "resnet18", "resnet50", "vits16", a torch.nn.Module,

a Backbone, a path to an .onnx file, or a function returning feature maps

'vitt16' training weights of a built-in model: "random", "imagenet" or "dino" (vitt16: random, imagenet) 'imagenet' layers built-in models: numbers (``[3, 4]``) or paper notation (``"N34"``, ``"N:9-12"``);

None: N34 for ResNets, the last block for ViTs. Other models: module names.

None k number of concepts per projector (an upper bound with projector="bayesian") 10 projector None/"kmeans", "bayesian" (Dirichlet-prior k-means, Gibbs sampling), "pca", or

a scikit-learn-style object. Clusterers assign a pixel to the closest prototype, projections (PCA, NMF, ...) to the component with the largest absolute value.

None bayes_alpha Dirichlet concentration, Gibbs sweeps and

discarded sweeps of projector="bayesian"

1.0 bayes_iter Dirichlet concentration, Gibbs sweeps and

discarded sweeps of projector="bayesian"

1.0 bayes_burn_in Dirichlet concentration, Gibbs sweeps and

discarded sweeps of projector="bayesian"

1.0 upsample "nearest" (default: the paper's blocky maps), "linear" or "cubic": interpolation of deeper

layers and of concept scores to pixels

'nearest' window "auto" (windows when the longer side is at least `window_factor` times the model's

input size, 224 px for the built-in models: windows twice the input size, every half window, each pixel from the window whose centre is nearest), None (always whole), or a window size in px

'auto' window_factor see `window` 3 features built-in ViTs: "tokens" (the blocks' outputs, default) or "keys" (the attention keys

of the same blocks, as in LOST and TokenCut). Saliency and class predictions always use the blocks' outputs, which the classifier reads.

'tokens' fit_on "all" (every composite pixel: exact if they fit in memory, else streamed through

mini-batch k-means, with a warning) or "sample" (sample_size composite pixels)

'all' sample_size composite pixels used with fit_on="sample" (and to seed streaming) 20000 epochs streaming passes when fit_on="all" falls back to mini-batch k-means 1 normalize per-pixel L2 normalisation of each layer (Algorithm 1, line 9) True scale C_min / (1 + C_b) scaling of each layer (Algorithm 1, line 10) True uncertainty_temp softmax temperature of the uncertainty (default 0.1). "auto": 1 for

probabilistic projectors, else the median gap between the two best concept scores

0.1 transforms "default" (ImageNet-style normalisation of the model) or a function, or a list

of functions applied in order, from image to image (e.g. a resizing lambda). They get an (H, W, 3) uint8 array. If the last one returns uint8 (or floats in [0, 1]), the model's default normalisation follows; otherwise its output is used as the normalised input. Use only resizing and colour operations: maps are returned at the original size.

'default' classifier for the classes, correlations and saliency: None (the model's own head), a

torch.nn.Linear, a (classes, C) weight matrix, a (weight, bias) pair, or a function image -> class scores or class id

None class_names names of the classes for `summarize` (a list or dict) None seed random seed 0 device for PyTorch models 'cpu' progress False, True (progress bar) or a callable(fraction, text) False Attributes (after fitting)

The NAVE explanation of one image.

Attributes:

Name Type Description explanation (H, W) int32, the concept of every pixel (the explanation map) uncertainty (H, W) float32 in [0, 1], normalised entropy of the concept assignment

(with uncertainty=True), else None

K number of concepts, e.g. for ``np.bincount(exp.explanation.ravel(), minlength=exp.K)``

docs.title: fit(images, groups=None, merge_groups=True, reorder='ward')
docs.text:
Extract concepts from images.

images : an (N, H, W, 3) or (N, H, W) array (uint8, or float in [0, 1]), or a list of images groups : one label per image: one projector is fitted per group, and the groups become the classes of the correlation merge_groups : merge the groups' projectors into one (predict then ignores groups) reorder : "ward", "average", "single" or None: order of the concept ids. With groups, concepts are ordered by group first, then within each group, and every group gets a colour family.

docs.title: update_patches(images, min_size=None)
docs.text:
Recompute the patches (closest and largest cell of every concept) on images.

min_size : minimum height and width, in pixels, of a cell to be the closest one. If no cell is large enough, the largest is used (with a warning); a concept with no cell at all gets an empty patch.

docs.title: predict(images, groups=None, uncertainty=False)
docs.text:
Explanations of images with the fitted concepts: a list of ImageExplanations.

groups : one label per image: use only that group's projector (when fitted with merge_groups=False). None: every projector scores every pixel, the closest wins. uncertainty : also compute the uncertainty map H(softmax(scores / T)) / log K

docs.title: fit_predict(images, groups=None, merge_groups=True, reorder='ward', uncertainty=False)
docs.text: fit, then predict on the same images.

docs.title: explain(images, uncertainty=False)
docs.text: Explain images: with the fitted concepts after an explicit fit, otherwise by fitting afresh on these images (every call). One image gives one ImageExplanation, several a list.

docs.title: segment(image)
docs.text: Superpixels: explain(image).segmentation().

docs.title: saliency(images, classifier=None, target=None)
docs.text:
Concept-based saliency: the cosine between the deepest layer's features and the classifier's vector of the target class, averaged over NAVE regions from the deepest layer to the shallowest. One (H, W) float32 map per image (a list for several).

classifier : as in the constructor (overrides it); None uses the constructor's, else the model's own head target : class index; None = the class the model predicts

docs.title: summarize(image, correlation=True, uncertainty=False, saliency=False, patches='closest', classifier=None, target=None, label=None, saliency_range=(-1, 1))
docs.text:
A figure in the style of the paper's Figure 1, for one image.

Row 1: the image | its explanation (uncertainty as opacity on white if asked) | its saliency (if asked), all at the image's size. Then, for every block of 10 concepts: their correlation with the classes (if available and asked) and their patches ("closest" or "largest"), framed in the concept's colour. Returns the matplotlib Figure. saliency_range : (vmin, vmax) of the saliency colours (default (-1, 1): saliency is a cosine), or "auto": centred on 0, up to the item's largest |saliency|

docs.title: segmentation()
docs.text: (H, W) int32 connected regions of the explanation map, like skimage.segmentation.slic.

docs.title: border(width=1)
docs.text: (H, W) int32 mask (0 and 1) of the inner margin, width px wide, of every region.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Built-in models, their blocks and the trainings with weights.

nave.models.available()["vits16"] {'blocks': 12, 'trainings': ('random', 'imagenet', 'dino'), 'default_blocks': [12]}

Download a built-in model's pretrained weights now, and return where they are.

nave-xai otherwise downloads them the first time a model needs them; call this ahead of time, for instance before working offline. They are kept in cache_dir() (NAVE_XAI_CACHE sets it).

from nave_xai import download_weights download_weights("vitt16", "imagenet") # ViT-Ti/16, about 11 MB, once

docs.title: How NAVE works
docs.text: NAVE explains a frozen vision encoder: it extracts concepts from the encoder's feature activations at several depths and maps them back onto the image. The explanation does not depend on a classifier or a label.

docs.title: Layers and composite pixels
docs.text:
An encoder is a stack of layers (blocks). Each outputs a feature map: a grid of positions, each with a vector of C numbers. A ResNet's four blocks halve the resolution each time:

Block Stride Grid at 448 px Channels (ResNet18 / 50) 1 4 112 x 112 64 / 256 2 8 56 x 56 128 / 512 3 16 28 x 28 256 / 1024 4 32 14 x 14 512 / 2048

ViT-Ti/16 and ViT-S/16 have 12 blocks, all on the same grid of 16 px patches (192 and 384 channels).

NAVE (Algorithm 1 of the paper) combines the chosen layers per position:

  1. Upsample every chosen layer to the grid of the shallowest one.
  2. Normalise each position's vector to length 1 (normalize=True).
  3. Scale each layer by C_min / (1 + C_b), so layers with many channels do not dominate (scale=True).
  4. Concatenate: each position becomes a composite pixel mixing detail and semantics.
  5. Project the composite pixels onto K concepts.

The paper's notation names the layers: N34 is blocks 3 and 4; N:9-12 is blocks 9 and 12.

For the built-in ViTs, features="keys" reads the attention keys of the chosen blocks instead of their outputs: each block's input after its layer norm, through the key projection, before attention mixes the tokens. This is what LOST and TokenCut use for object discovery with DINO. Saliency and class predictions still use the blocks' outputs, which the classifier reads. normalize=False and scale=False reproduce the paper's ablations.

docs.title: Projectors
docs.text:
projector= None / "kmeans" k-means++ seeding and Lloyd iterations; prototypes are the centroids "bayesian" k-means with a Dirichlet prior on the weights, by Gibbs sampling; k is an upper bound "pca" principal components; a pixel goes to the component with the largest absolute projection any object scikit-learn style: clusterers (predict + transform, predict_proba, or fit_predict) or projections (transform only: PCA, NMF, ICA)

Bayesian k-means is a finite approximation of a Dirichlet-process mixture: π ~ Dirichlet(α/K), z ~ Categorical(π), x ~ N(μ_z, σ²I) with one shared σ². Assignments are sampled with the cluster means integrated out, leaving each point out of its own cluster, so duplicate clusters merge and the number of concepts used is learned. After bayes_burn_in sweeps, posterior means are averaged and pixels assigned with them; concepts below 0.5% of the posterior weight are dropped. It runs on sample_size composite pixels.

docs.title: From the grid to pixels
docs.text: Concepts are extracted on the feature grid, coarser than the image. nave-xai interpolates the concept scores to pixel resolution and takes the best concept per pixel: the explanation map. With upsample="nearest" this gives the paper's blocky maps; "linear" and "cubic" smooth boundaries. One concept can appear in several places; segmentation() gives the connected regions.

docs.title: Uncertainty
docs.text: With uncertainty=True, every pixel gets H(softmax(scores / T)) / log K, the normalised entropy of its concept assignment, from 0 (one concept clearly wins) to 1 (all equally likely). For k-means, scores are minus the squared distances to the prototypes, so 1 - uncertainty = 1 - H(softmax(-d² / T)) / log K is the certainty. The temperature T is uncertainty_temp, 0.1 by default; "auto" uses T = 1 for probabilistic projectors and otherwise the median gap between the two best concept scores.

docs.title: Ordering and colours
docs.text:
After fitting, concepts are renumbered along a dendrogram of their prototypes (reorder="ward" in fit). Ward linkage is exact from prototypes and concept sizes: the cost of merging two clusters, n_a n_b / (n_a + n_b) |c_a - c_b|², depends only on their centroids and sizes. "average" and "single" linkage use distances between prototypes. With groups, concepts are ordered by group first, and every group gets a colour family.

reorder(by="classes") groups concepts under the class they correlate with most (from correlation), unassigned ones last; recolor=True gives every class a colour and its concepts shades of it (color_vary, color_spread).

docs.title: Patches and correlation
docs.text: A cell is a connected region of an explanation map assigned to one concept. For every concept, the closest cell (smallest mean distance of its composite pixels to the prototype) and the largest cell of the fitting set are kept as patches: 32 x 32 views, dimmed outside the cell, with a 1 px white line around it. correlation is the Pearson correlation, across images, between a concept's proportion in an image and the image's class (the groups given to fit, else the model's prediction).

docs.title: Concept-based saliency
docs.text:
saliency(image) explains a class with the encoder's own regions:

  1. At every position of the deepest chosen layer (before pooling), take the cosine between the feature vector and the classifier's weight vector of the target class.
  2. Explain that layer alone with NAVE and average the cosine over each region.
  3. Move one layer shallower: upsample, explain with the cumulative layers (N4, then N34, then N234) and average per region again.
  4. Upsample the result to the image.

docs.title: Your own models
docs.text: Any encoder that turns an image into feature maps can be explained. Pass it as model= and name its layers.

docs.title: PyTorch
docs.text:
pip install "nave-xai[torch]"

import torchvision
from nave_xai import NAVEImage

model = torchvision.models.resnet101(weights="DEFAULT")
exp = NAVEImage(model, layers=["layer3", "layer4"], k=10).explain(image)

Layers are module names from model.named_modules(): "layer3" (torchvision ResNet), "features.5" (torchvision ConvNeXt), "blocks.11" (timm ViT), "encoder.layer.11" (Hugging Face ViT). Their outputs are captured with forward hooks during one forward pass. Token outputs (N, L, C) are reshaped to the patch grid after dropping class and register tokens.

For more control, build the backbone yourself:

from nave_xai.models import TorchBackbone

backbone = TorchBackbone(
    model,
    mean=(0.485, 0.456, 0.406), std=(0.229, 0.224, 0.225),   # the model's normalisation
    multiple=16,             # input sides must be multiples of this (patch size for ViTs)
    patch_size=16,           # token outputs: patch size (found automatically if omitted)
    prefix_tokens=1,         # class + register tokens before the patches (found automatically)
    classifier="head",       # for classes and saliency: module name or a torch.nn.Linear
    final_norm="norm",       # norm the classifier reads after (ViTs)
    device="cuda",
)
NAVEImage(backbone, layers=["blocks.8", "blocks.11"])

docs.title: ONNX
docs.text:
from nave_xai.models import OnnxBackbone
NAVEImage(OnnxBackbone("encoder.onnx", blocks=["stage3", "stage4"], multiple=32), layers=["stage3", "stage4"])

The model's first input takes the normalised image (1, 3, H, W); the named outputs are the layers, each (1, C, h, w).

docs.title: Any function (JAX, TensorFlow, ...)
docs.text:
from nave_xai.models import FunctionBackbone

def features(x):                       # x: float32 (1, 3, H, W), already normalised
    return {"mid": mid_features(x), "deep": deep_features(x)}     # numpy (1, C, h, w)

NAVEImage(FunctionBackbone(features, blocks=["mid", "deep"], multiple=32), layers=["mid", "deep"])

docs.title: Fitting on a dataset
docs.text:
fit extracts one set of concepts from many images; predict then explains any image with them, so a concept means the same thing in every image.

from nave_xai import NAVEImage

explainer = NAVEImage(model="resnet50", k=10).fit(images)     # (N, H, W, 3) array or list of images
explanations = explainer.predict(test_images)             # a list of Explanations
exp = explainer.explain(test_images[0])                   # one image: one Explanation

Images keep their size (larger ones are processed in windows). To resize them, use transforms=.

docs.title: What fit computes
docs.text:
Attribute prototypes (K, D) concept prototypes palette (K, 3) concept colours patches (K, 2, 32, 32, 3) closest and largest cell of every concept classes the groups given to fit, else the model's predicted classes correlation (K, C) correlation of concept proportions with classes fitted True

With fit_on="all" (default) every composite pixel is used: exactly when they fit in half the free memory, otherwise streamed through mini-batch k-means, with a warning (PCA is accumulated exactly either way). fit_on="sample" uses sample_size random composite pixels.

Classes come from the model's own head (the built-in ImageNet models, PyTorch models that output class scores) or from classifier=: a torch.nn.Linear, a weight matrix, or a function from image to class scores.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
explainer.fit(images, groups=labels)                       # one projector per group
explainer.fit(images, groups=labels, merge_groups=False)   # keep them apart
explainer.predict(images, groups=labels)                   # each image with its group's concepts

This is the paper's protocol: one k-means per class, merged. Concepts are numbered by group, and every group gets a colour family; classes and correlation use the groups. With merge_groups=False, predict(groups=...) uses only each image's group; without groups every projector scores every pixel and the closest concept wins.

docs.title: Ordering and colours
docs.text:
explainer.reorder("ward")                                       # or "average", "single", or a list
explainer.reorder(by="classes", recolor=True)                   # grouped and coloured by class
explainer.reorder(by="classes", recolor=True, color_vary=["lightness", "saturation"], color_spread=0.7)
explainer.set_palette("tab20")                                  # Spectral by default; or a (K, 3) uint8 array

Without recolor, colours follow their concepts.

docs.title: Patches
docs.text:
explainer.update_patches(other_images, min_size=48)      # cells at least 48 x 48 px for "closest"

If no cell is large enough, the largest is used (with a warning); a concept without any cell gets an empty patch.

docs.title: Saliency and summary
docs.text:
maps = explainer.saliency(images)                   # one (H, W) map per image
explainer.summarize(image, uncertainty=True, saliency=True, patches="closest")

summarize draws, for one image, the image | its explanation | its saliency, all at the image's size; then, for every block of 10 concepts, their correlation with the classes and their patches framed in their colour, as in the paper's Figure 1.

The correlation needs several images with at least two different classes. When there is none (one image, or a single class), that row shows instead each concept's mean saliency in the summarized image (with a classifier), so the concepts can still be related to the prediction. Saliency is a cosine and is always shown on [-1, 1]. With uncertainty=True, uncertain pixels of the explanation fade to white.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
nave-xai is on PyPI:

pip install nave-xai               # numpy, onnxruntime, matplotlib; ViT-Ti/16's weights download on first use
pip install "nave-xai[torch]"      # also your own PyTorch models, GPU

docs.title: 1. Explain an image
docs.text:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.image import imread
from nave_xai import NAVEImage

image = imread("photo.jpg")              # (H, W, 3), uint8 or float in [0, 1]; PIL images work too
explainer = NAVEImage()                       # ViT-Ti/16 trained on ImageNet (weights download once, about 11 MB)
exp = explainer.explain(image)

plt.imshow(explainer.palette[exp.explanation])   # every concept in its colour

exp is an ImageExplanation:

explanation (H, W) int32: the concept of every pixel uncertainty (H, W) float32 in [0, 1], with explain(image, uncertainty=True) K the number of concepts segmentation() (H, W) connected regions of the explanation map, like skimage.segmentation.slic border(width=1) (H, W) 0/1 mask of every region's inner margin

The share of each concept in the image is np.bincount(exp.explanation.ravel(), minlength=exp.K) divided by the number of pixels.

Without a previous fit, explain fits on the image it is given, at every call. After fit(images), it explains with the fitted concepts.

docs.title: 2. Draw it
docs.text:
nave-xai returns arrays; draw them with any tool:

colours = explainer.palette[exp.explanation]                   # (H, W, 3) uint8
picture = colours.copy()
picture[exp.border(2) == 1] = 255                              # white region borders
plt.imshow(picture)

u = explainer.explain(image, uncertainty=True).uncertainty
plt.imshow((1 - u)[..., None] * colours / 255 + u[..., None])   # fades to white where uncertain

For a ready-made figure, explainer.summarize(image) shows the image, its explanation, the correlation of the concepts with the classes, and every concept's patch.

docs.title: 3. What to explain
docs.text:
NAVEImage(
    model="resnet50",        # "vitt16" (default), "resnet18", "resnet50", "vits16", or your own model
    training="imagenet",     # "random", "imagenet", "dino"
    layers=[3, 4],           # or "N34"; ViT: e.g. [9, 12] or "N:9-12"
    k=10,                    # concepts
    upsample="nearest",      # default, blocky as in the paper; or "linear", "cubic"
)
  • Layers: shallow layers carry detail and edges, deep layers semantics; their combination is what makes NAVE's concepts informative. By default: N34 for ResNets, the last block for ViTs.
  • k sets the granularity of the explanation.
  • upsample controls how concept scores go from the feature grid to pixels.

docs.title: 4. Concepts across images
docs.text:
explainer = NAVEImage(model="resnet50", k=10).fit(images)
explanations = explainer.predict(other_images)          # a list of Explanations
explainer.summarize(other_images[0], saliency=True)

See Fitting on a dataset.

docs.title: 5. Preprocessing
docs.text:
By default, images are normalised as the model expects (ImageNet mean and standard deviation). transforms= replaces that with a function, or a list of functions, from image to image:

from PIL import Image
half = lambda im: np.asarray(Image.fromarray(im).resize((im.shape[1] // 2, im.shape[0] // 2)))
NAVEImage(transforms=half)        # explained at half size; maps come back at the original size

If the last function returns uint8 (or floats in [0, 1]), the model's normalisation follows; if it returns normalised floats, they are used as they are. Use only resizing and colour operations.

docs.title: 6. Large images
docs.text: An image goes through the encoder whole unless its longer side reaches three times the model's input size (672 px for the built-in models). Larger images are processed in overlapping windows, so memory stays bounded and the encoder sees them at a scale close to its training. See Memory and large images.

docs.title: Working offline
docs.text:
Pretrained weights are downloaded the first time a model needs them, then kept in a cache. To download them ahead, for instance before working offline:

from nave_xai import download_weights
download_weights("vitt16", "imagenet")     # about 11 MB; also "resnet18", "resnet50", "vits16" with "imagenet" or "dino"

The cache is ~/.cache/nave-xai on Linux (NAVE_XAI_CACHE sets another folder).

docs.title: Inspecting models
docs.text:
NAVE explanations reflect what an encoder learned, which makes them a diagnostic tool (Sections 4 and 5 of the paper). Each recipe below is a notebook in notebooks/inspecting/. Notebooks 4 and 9 need PyTorch; the others run with the built-in encoders.

Notebook Question 01_training.ipynb How do random, supervised (ImageNet) and self-supervised (DINO) training shape the concepts? 02_architectures.ipynb Do a ResNet and a ViT decompose the same image the same way? 03_depth.ipynb How do concepts change from shallow to deep blocks, and where is information compressed? 04_vit_registers.ipynb Do high-norm token artifacts of ViTs form concepts, and do registers remove them? (PyTorch) 05_shortcuts.ipynb Does a shortcut (a watermark) take over the explanation? 06_concept_features.ipynb Are concept proportions informative enough for a classifier probe? 07_localization.ipynb Can a concept's region localize an object (inner and outer boxes)? 08_uncertainty.ipynb Where does the encoder hesitate between concepts? 09_causality.ipynb Do the concepts that come with a class actually drive its score? (PyTorch)

docs.title: Concepts and causality
docs.text:
NAVE's correlation tells which concepts come with a class, not whether the model uses them. 09_causality.ipynb asks the causal question with interventions, for a pretrained ResNet50 and a ViT-S/16. At one block, a forward hook replaces the tokens of a concept with those of other images at the same positions (resampling ablation) and lets the network run on; the drop in the true class's logit is the concept's effect. Replacing as many random tokens the same way gives a control, and a concept's causal effect is its effect beyond that control, averaged over the images where it appears, with bootstrap intervals. The notebook then sets correlation against causal effect, concept by concept, and shows where they disagree: context that comes with a class but is ignored, and features the model uses without their being specific to a class.

The effect is causal for the model, not for the world, and interventions shift the activations' distribution; the notebook ends with these caveats.

docs.title: How images are processed
docs.text:
Image window="auto" does longer side below window_factor (3) times the model's input size (672 px for the built-in models) the whole image in one forward pass larger windows twice the input size (448 px), every half window (224 px)

Every pixel comes from the window whose centre is nearest, so no pixel is read close to a window's edge, where features are distorted: each window keeps its central half (margins of about a quarter of the window, rounded to the model's feature grid). Concepts are fitted on all windows together, so they mean the same everywhere in the image. Models tied to one input size use windows of that size.

The network also needs image sides that are multiples of its downsampling (32 for ResNets, 16 for ViTs), so images are padded by mirroring their edges, and the maps cropped back.

The class an image is predicted to be (for classes and correlation) is the average of the windows' logits, each weighted by its share of real, not padded, pixels. Whole-image methods (saliency) run on the image resized to at most 1024 px, and their map is resized back.

NAVEImage(window=None)           # always whole
NAVEImage(window=640)            # your window size (a multiple of 32)
NAVEImage(window_factor=5)       # windows only from five times the input size

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Composite pixels are produced a few rows at a time (about 64 MB per chunk), so peak memory is set by one window, not by the image. What grows:

  • ViT attention grows with the square of the number of patches in a window.
  • ResNet block 1 has a grid 16 times larger than block 3.
  • fit_on="all" stores every composite pixel when they fit in half the free memory, and otherwise streams them through mini-batch k-means, with a warning.

Before a run, nave-xai estimates its peak memory and issues a NaveMemoryWarning if it may not fit.

import warnings
from nave_xai import NaveMemoryWarning
warnings.simplefilter("error", NaveMemoryWarning)      # turn the warning into an error

docs.title: Time series
docs.text:
NAVESeries explains encoders of time series (1D CNNs, transformers): one concept per time step, shared by all channels, since the encoder mixes them. The ECG version of the method is described in Boubekki et al., Explaining deep learning for ECG using time-localized clusters (arXiv:2509.15198).

from nave_xai import NAVESeries

explainer = NAVESeries(model, layers=["block3", "block4", "block5"], k=20, multiple=8).fit(series)
exp = explainer.explain(series[0], uncertainty=True)
exp.explanation          # (T,) the concept of every time step
exp.segments()           # (T,) runs of steps with the same concept
exp.border()             # (T,) 1 at change points
explainer.summarize(series[0], uncertainty=True, saliency=True)

docs.title: Inputs and models
docs.text:
Series are channels first, as in PyTorch: an (N, C, T) array, a list of (C, T_i) arrays of different lengths, or one (C, T) or (T,) series. transforms= applies functions to each (C, T) series (normalisation, filtering); there is none by default.

model is a torch.nn.Module (layers are module names; channels_last=True for transformer layers that output (N, t, C)), an .onnx file (layers are output names), or any function x (1, C, T) -> {layer: (C_b, t_b) array}; a function may also return the class scores under "logits". multiple= is the model's total downsampling: inputs are padded (mirrored) to a multiple of it.

docs.title: Long series
docs.text: With window=W (steps), series longer than W are processed in windows of W steps every W/2 steps; every step comes from the window whose centre is nearest, far from any window edge.

docs.title: What fit computes
docs.text:
As for images, prototypes, palette, classes (groups or the model's predictions) and correlation; instead of image patches, for every concept:

snippets the segments closest to the prototype, with context, all channels profiles (K, C, 40, 3): 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of its segments, resampled to 40 points positions (K, 12): where its segments sit in the series durations (K, 2): median and mean segment length, in steps

update_snippets(series) recomputes them on other series.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
summarize(series) draws one row per channel with the signal over the segmentation, an uncertainty row (uncertainty=True; bright = certain, black = uncertain), a saliency row (saliency=True, standardized then passed through a sigmoid, as in the ECG paper), the correlation of the concepts with the classes, and for every concept its position and duration, its snippets and its profile, one band per channel, 10 concepts per row. span=(start, end) zooms on part of a long series; label= adds the true class next to the model's prediction in the title.

See notebooks/series.ipynb for a complete example on BasicMotions (smartwatch motions).

Without correlation (one item, or a single class), the summary shows each concept's mean saliency in the item instead, on [-1, 1] (it needs a classifier).

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
NAVEText explains text encoders: one concept per token.

from nave_xai import NAVEText

explainer = NAVEText("spacy").fit(documents)            # pip install "nave-xai[text]"
exp = explainer.explain("Oil prices rose after OPEC cut production.", uncertainty=True)
list(zip(exp.tokens, exp.explanation))
explainer.summarize(documents[0], saliency=True, classifier=head)

docs.title: Inputs and models
docs.text:
A string is one document and a list of strings several; an already tokenized document is a list of tokens, so several of them are a list of lists.

  • model="spacy": spaCy's tok2vec encoder of en_core_web_sm (hashed embeddings, then four residual window-CNN blocks of 96 channels; MIT license). Install it with pip install "nave-xai[text]", then python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm (about 12 MB). Layers are "block1" to "block4"; by default blocks 2 to 4. Its tokenizer is used.
  • Any function tokens -> {layer: (C_b, n_tokens) array}, optionally with the class scores under "logits". PyTorch and Hugging Face models are wrapped in such a function (tokens to ids inside).

Text needs more concepts than images: the default is k=20. With few concepts, the tokens a classifier relies on most (the topic keywords) tend to share one concept whatever the topic; groups= (one projector per class) or more concepts separate them.

docs.title: What fit computes
docs.text:
As for images, prototypes, palette, classes and correlation; for every concept:

span_counts number of spans (runs of consecutive tokens with the concept) mean_runs mean number of consecutive tokens with the concept words its characteristic words: frequency in the concept relative to overall spans its spans closest to the prototype, with context

update_spans(texts) recomputes them on other texts.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
summarize(text) shows the document wrapped, each token on its concept's colour with the background's opacity = certainty; with saliency=True, the font size shows the saliency's magnitude and black / white its sign. Then the correlation of the concepts with the classes, and one row per concept: colour, spans and mean run, characteristic words and its two closest spans in context. label= adds the true class next to the model's prediction in the title. reorder(by="classes", recolor=True) is recommended for text: every class gets its colour family, so a document's topic shows at a glance.

See notebooks/text.ipynb for a complete example on Reuters news.

Without correlation (one item, or a single class), the summary shows each concept's mean saliency in the item instead, on [-1, 1] (it needs a classifier).
